newsitem.title: FRANCE: OPINION-OFCE's Philippe Sigogne on France and EMU.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-OFCE's Philippe Sigogne on France and EMU.

text.p: By Philippe Sigogne, director of forecasting at France's OFCE economic research institute
PARIS, Oct 1 - The French government's announcement of its draft 1997 budget turned out to be a non-event, which doesn't seem to surprise anyone any more.

However loudly a radical fringe in Germany's opposition SPD denounces with virtuous indignation the accounting tricks used by the French state, the financial markets have been unmoved. Yet just a month ago, the general feeling was that the franc would be specially under pressure during the budget debate.

So were dealers just up to their usual trick of inventing something to shake trading volumes out of their torpor? Or have the markets capitulated to the unflinching determination of the Franco-German partners, who hold the reins of power and keep reasserting their certainty of reaching the goal on schedule?

In hindsight, it's not difficult to find plenty of reasons why the financial community should welcome the draft budget relatively positively. Firstly, the U.S. economy is pushing up the dollar, whether or not the Fed effectively tightens monetary policy. Everyone realises that the Fed is acting, or will act, preventively and that the inflationary risk is very slight. The franc can only benefit from that situation.

Recent balance of payments figures show a considerable capital outflow in the first half of 1996: 200 billion francs from residents on top of 90 billion francs from non-residents. That trend, due to France's specific economic and labour problems, cannot continue at that rate and is bound to give way to a considerable influx.

Economic activity may rebound when the end of de-stocking automatically improves the mood of companies and consumers. That is one of the necessary, if not sufficient conditions to stop the automatic increase in the budget deficit and give the state some hope of success in reducing public spending.

Other factors include the impact of the fall in interest rates on the cost of servicing public debt. Debt can be refinanced today at rates close to six percent against around nine percent for expiring long-term debt, and short-term debt at rates of around 3.5-4.0 percent instead of six percent last year. Thus for the first time debt service is actually contributing to braking public spending instead of increasing it.

Franco-German comparisons are less disadvantageous to France than they appeared when the Germans were preparing their package of savings measures. There is definitely a concern on the other side of the Rhine to pursue rigour without ruining the recovery, so much so that the DIW institute in Berlin even calls the 1997 budget slightly expansionary.

Governments are thinking the same way as markets: it's better not to stifle the recovery just when it is starting to appear, but to get over 1997 by making the most of cashflow expedients. Pretending to respect the criteria is thus seen as the best way of satisfying both the letter and the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty.

This leeway given to states whose participation is considered indispensible to the launch of the single currency is not however a blank cheque. The final objective is and remains to stabilise public debt as a percentage of GDP. Hence the importance of the stability pact intended to reassure markets for the future.

The sustained weakness of the European economy cannot be invoked indefinitely to justify indiscipline. On the contrary. The slowdown in investment which began in 1991 and spread in 1993 has significantly reduced the European Union's growth potential, which is now only two percent a year, compared to the three percent hoped for when the convergence criteria were set.

The impact on public accounts, compounded by a further decline in inflation, is that sustainable deficits should no longer exceed 2.0-2.5 percent instead of the Maastricht three percent to stabilise public debt at 60 percent of GDP.

The obvious danger of an implosion inherent if this accounting method were applied literally just shows the need to find a different way out: dynamising private investment to increase the potential for growth and minimise the share of new savings grabbed by the public sector. That is the real yardstick by which governments and their currency will be measured.
